edge.title: The big order with no money yet
edge.setup: A buyer you have never dealt with asks for a large lot at a good rate. They want delivery first and promise payment later: a cheque, a transfer 'by evening', or 'once we sell it on'. Perhaps a small earlier order was paid on time, which is why this one feels safe.
edge.tell: A new buyer who wants the goods first and the money later is asking you to be their lender.
move: Release goods only against money that has cleared in your own account, not a screenshot, a cheque or a promise.
Keep first deals small and split large lots into instalments, each released after the previous one is paid.
Check the firm through an independent source, and call the number you find yourself rather than the one they gave you.
If it goes wrong, file a police complaint quickly with the chats, invoices and vehicle details.
edge.why: Credit fraud works because the seller's wish for volume overrides the ordinary question of whether this stranger is good for the money. A small early order paid on time buys trust cheaply, and the large one is where the fraudster collects. The defence is to treat every unpaid delivery as a loan and decide whether you would lend that much to that person.
edge.variants: Same shape: a freelancer asked to deliver the full work before any advance, a shop asked to hand over stock on 'consignment', a landlord handing over keys against a promised deposit.

scenario.question: A new buyer wants 200 units at a good rate, delivered today, and promises the transfer 'by evening'. Their small order last week was paid on time. What do you do?

choices.text: Offer to send the first instalment of the lot once the money has cleared in your own bank account, and the rest after each payment clears.
Send the full lot today; last week's order proves they pay.
Accept a post-dated cheque for the full amount and deliver everything.

lens.name: Loss aversion
lens.one_line: Losing ₹1,000 hurts about twice as much as gaining ₹1,000 pleases — and salespeople know it.
lens.detail: The same offer framed as a loss moves people far harder than framed as a gain, so persuasion is engineered to make inaction feel like losing something: expiring offers, 'you'll lose your spot', free trials that auto-convert once the thing feels yours. Noticing the frame restores the actual choice underneath it.
elsewhere: 'Only 2 left at this price' converting far better than a discount.
Holding a falling stock to avoid realising a loss.
Free trials relying on the pain of giving something up.
lens.test: Is this being framed as something I'd lose? Restate it as a plain gain and see if I still want it.
lens.today: The Hindu and the Times of India report that BDA has halved regularisation charges, a 50% cut in guidance value, and is inviting applications for absolute sale deeds. A half-price window is a loss frame: the pull is 'don't miss it', not 'do I need this'. If you hold a BDA site, restate it as a plain gain (what a clear title gets you, at what cost) and decide on that, using BDA's own notice rather than an agent's pitch.
